Composed by Śākyabuddhi at Hongfa Monastery in the Imperial Capital.
There was a young gentleman of worldly standing who, feeling some stagnation, questioned the Master of the Pure Land, saying: "I have heard that the Buddha-dharma is profound and empty."
The path of language is severed;
the Dharma-gate is profound and concise;
the sphere of mental activity is extinguished.
These words arise from deluded sentiments;
every mental activity is nothing but inverted perception.
Now you wish to rely on a western realm solely to extol Amitābha.
The claim that the path is severed may well be incorrect;
the assertion that one dwells in cessation is rarely true.
It is simply that their minds remain close to stagnation and have not yet reached the Great Vehicle.
Please knock on the Thunder Gate to open these hibernating chambers; yet,
within this realm, there is no impurity.
Purify this very mind;
direct your thoughts toward the Western Quarter;
clarify what has not yet been clarified.
The ten directions are entirely pure;
yet you focus only on a single corner,
employing such biased attachments to your emotions.
"I pray that you will explain this for me.
The Master said, "How timely is your question!"
Who but a wise man could demonstrate this?
Yet the profundity of the Dharma-gate is truly as the Tathāgata’s intent declares.
In the end, I am ashamed of my own lack of agility;
yet, I shall attempt to discuss this further.
Now, those who have attained the Way find great benefit in being seen.
Everything before one's eyes is thus.
Yet the wisdom of ordinary people is shallow;
wherever they encounter it, they give rise to stagnation.
However, according to the grand regulations of the Noble Teachings,
the ranks are categorized at eighty thousand;
yet, to discuss them in brief:
There is no principle that transcends these two gates;
they are like the two wheels of a chariot or the two wings of a bird.
If either one is lacking, one cannot soar aloft in empty tranquility;
as stated in the *Awakening of Faith*, there are two gates: calming (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Cessation (śamatha) takes principle as its object;
contemplation (vipaśyanā) takes phenomena as its object.
If one has not yet mastered these two...
Thus, one merely constructs emptiness and gives rise to stagnation.
That speech ceases and the mind is extinguished is the principle;
that one anticipates the West and recites the Buddha's name is the practice.
However, since the three realms are mind-only,
the domain within is not defiled;
yet, if one has not yet attained the tenth stage, [one cannot transcend it].
Furthermore, as for purifying the mind through objects:
although the ten directions are all pure,
the objects of perception are universally dispersed.
Because one wishes to cause focused contemplation on rebirth there, one has thus exclusively examined this single corner [of the teaching]. Chapter One:
The Essential Nature of the Land of Certainty (Niyata-bhūmi). I. Clarifying the Essential Nature. II. Clarifying whether it is Included or Excluded from the Three Realms. Question:
The gates of that land are trodden by both ordinary beings and sages alike;
such is the precious realm of Amitābha.
If one can ascend by means of ten recitations,
and since it is permitted that both the great and the small may travel there together so that all classes of beings may go in unison,
I do not yet know what the essential nature and the physical characteristics of that land are like.
The answer is:
Now, gaudy colors dazzle the eyes,
and clever words obscure the principles.
Now, wishing to enable both the ignorant and the wise to understand alike,
I have for the time being eliminated superfluous rhetoric and shall explain by pointing directly to the essential meaning.
First, regarding the clarification of the essential nature,
there are three sections.
The first is the pure land of the dharmakāya.
Second, the pure land of the reward body;
third, the pure land of the transformation body.
Regarding the pure land of the dharma body:
There are two meanings:
first, it reveals the essence of the person who dwells;
second, it reveals the essence of the land in which they dwell.
Regarding those who are able to abide [in this teaching],
the *Awakening of Faith* explains the Tathāgatagarbha based upon it.
The essence possesses three great meanings.
The first is the meaning of the greatness of essence (*tattva-mahatva*);
it refers to all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*).
Because True Suchness (*tathatā*) is equal and neither increases nor decreases,
it is precisely this single-flavored True Suchness.
Furthermore, why would its essence not encompass both the internal and the external?
It also penetrates through both the ordinary and the holy.
Second is the meaning of the greatness of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇamahātva*),
which refers to the fact that the Tathāgatagarbha is fully endowed with the qualities of untainted nature (*anāsravadharmasvabhāva*).
This is precisely the meaning of the distinctions among the myriad virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
This exists where there are sentient beings;
it does not exist where there are insentient things.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"That which is not Buddha-nature refers to insentient things such as walls, tiles, and rubble."
Third is the function of the great meaning (*mahārtha*).
This refers to its ability to produce the causes and fruits of both mundane and supramundane virtue;
this is precisely the aforementioned function of the characteristics and place.
Now, since both great meanings are employed as the human body that abides,
they are discussed in their distinctions while existing within a single flavor.
Second, regarding the substance of the land where one dwells:
this takes the previously mentioned meaning of the "substantial greatness" (tǐdà) of the single-flavored true thusness (zhēnrú) as the substance of the land where one dwells.
This means that because it serves as the basis for the myriad virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
this constitutes the division of the two meanings of the identity between the person and the land.
Regarding the Pure Land of the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya),
there are two types: first,
the Land of True Reward (sambhoga-kṣetra).
Second is the land of phenomenal function.
As for the Land of Real Reward,
it is also identical in substance to the human realm.
This means that the initial arising of the myriad virtues constitutes the substance of that land.
As it is said in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* regarding the eighteen aspects of perfect purity:
The Great Emptiness and the Signless serve as the gateways,
and the three types of wisdom serve as the path;
this is also taught in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra.
The "garden of dhāraṇīs" refers to the forest trees of the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas and so forth.
As for those who are able to dwell therein:
Thus, by encompassing all myriad virtues,
one becomes a Buddha-person.
Such a person and their land—
All bodhisattvas from the lowest stages up to those at the level of the Vajra-mind cannot see it either;
only Buddhas can see one another.
Regarding the statement that "the land is used as the object," this refers to the distinct substantiality of the human realm and the land,
such as the Vairocana Lotus Treasury World and so forth.
Because it constitutes the substance of the land where one dwells, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"The pure land is characterized by the king of lotuses."
It serves as the basis of reliance.
Great meditative concentration, great compassion, and the wondrous physical marks and signs are that which constitute the human body capable of abiding therein.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"The Saṃbhogakāya has great meditative concentration and great compassion as its essence."
This person and this land can be seen,
according to their respective capacities, by Bodhisattvas from the first bhūmi upward.
Up to the tenth stage,
their visions are all different;
that is to say, the stages themselves are distinguished by being higher or lower.
There is also a distinction between the coarse and the subtle in terms of perception.
Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"If one excludes the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), [it is perceived] only by bodhisattvas from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward."
The provisions for enlightenment are thus not fully complete;
this is sometimes called the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) or the *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body).
Alternatively, it is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body). "Recompense" (*pā*) refers to returning;
responding to principle is termed "response" (*saṃ*).
Partaking of the flavors for the sake of others is called "enjoyment," or it is termed the "body of enjoyment" (saṃbhogakāya).
Similar to the enjoyment [body],
the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) and its pure land also have two types.
First, the three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* of altruistic practice;
"containing" refers to the constant transformation [of beings],
as well as this body and its land.
In this realm and in other directions, these appear constantly and without interruption—
whether for a single kalpa or a hundred years—
in the form of the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, and so forth.
This refers to the arising of things moment by moment and their repeated passing into nirvana.
Second is transformation, which is the sudden appearance of what previously did not exist.
This refers to relying upon this transformation body to further give rise to many other transformations,
as in the case of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
This refers to the constant manifestation of transformations.
To further give rise to emanated bodies is precisely the transformation of that which is non-existent suddenly becoming existent.
Sometimes he manifests in the forms of monkeys, deer, horses, and so forth;
it is not necessarily only as a Buddha. Since there are thus two types of bodies, [the distinction between them is established].
The same applies to the land.
Just as the various exquisite lotus flowers in the world of Abhirati,
these are the pure lands that constantly accompany the transformations [of the Buddha].
As it is said in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra:
when the Tathāgata pressed the earth with his toe,
the three thousandfold world-system was entirely purified.
This refers to the transformation of a pure land from non-existence to sudden existence.
These two bodies and two lands are accessible only to bodhisattvas prior to the stages (bhūmi).
It can be seen by those of the two vehicles and by ordinary beings.
Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"If one were apart from the nirmāṇakāya..."
The Śrāvakas are emaciated and coarse;
likewise, those in the stage of aspiring and delighting, as well as those who have newly resolved their minds to practice,
do not achieve accomplishment.

The Dharma-body and its land are perceived by the wisdom-eye, the Dharma-eye, and the Buddha-eye among the five eyes; the retribution-body and transformation-body lands are likewise perceived [by these].
This refers to what is seen by the fleshly eye and the divine eye.
A question is asked:
"Since there are three kinds of lands, [how is this so?]"
It was not known what kind of land the Western region was.
He replied,
"It also possesses three kinds."
If it is the vision of the fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of a bodhisattva who has already entered the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) and beyond,
this is the pure land of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
If it is the vision of the preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*) or the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), [it is otherwise].
This is the Pure Land of the Reward Body (*sambhogakāya*).
If it is seen by Bodhisattvas prior to the [first] stage, by those of the Two Vehicles, or by ordinary beings,
it is the Pure Land of the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
For instance, when Bodhisattvas such as Nāgārjuna were reborn there,
they fully perceived the three types of pure lands— the Dharma, Retribution, and Transformation lands—
because by virtue of their superior state, they were able to perceive those below.
For this reason, in various sūtras and śāstras,
it is sometimes judged to be retribution (vipāka).
Some judge it to be a transformation [body];
all of these do not miss the essential point. Question:
It is already known that the Western Quarter possesses three lands;
however, it remains unknown which land an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) who practices mindfulness of the Buddha with the aspiration for rebirth will attain.
The answer is as follows:
According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
it speaks only of the transformation land (*nirmāṇakṣetra*),
and does not mention the dharma body or reward lands (*dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*).
Within the transformed lands, there are two types:
first, birth from a womb;
second, miraculous birth.
Regarding those born from the soil,
there are further two types:
first, those who harbor doubts.
Born within a palace of the seven treasures in a border city of Sukhāvatī,
they do not see the Buddha for five hundred years;
this is called the "womb" (garbha).
This is what is taught in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* regarding the second [type of birth],
which is called "womb-birth" (*garbha*) because it truly possesses parents; as stated in the *Dundubhisvararāja-dhāraṇī-sūtra*.
This means that Amitābha Buddha likewise has parents and so forth.
A sutra states:
"The city is named Qingtai (Pure Peace)."
It was ten thousand yojanas in extent, filled with the Kṣatriya caste;
his father was named Candrottara, a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin).
His mother was named Viśeṣamukhā;
his son was named Candraprabha;
and these were the disciples who served him.
His name was Vimalakīrti;
his disciple preeminent in wisdom was named Prabhāsa;
and his disciple preeminent in supernormal powers was named Vaśavartin.
The name of Māra is "Invincible.

Devadatta's name is "Tranquility"; he is one who personally transforms all sentient beings through his own distinct manifestations, and is not one who attains rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha in the present age.
This refers to the single location;
it is only that there are perceived differences. Regarding the land of transformation-birth (*upapāduka*), according to the sūtras and śāstras:
There are three types:
first, lands that are exclusively Mahāyāna;
second, lands that are exclusively Hīnayāna.
Third, there are lands where the Great and Small Vehicles are mixed.
Regarding those that are exclusively Mahāyāna lands:
the sentient beings in these places...
Those who study exclusively the Mahāyāna will be reborn in that land;
these are like the three superior grades among the nine grades of rebirth.
Therefore, the *Wangsheng lun* (Treatise on Rebirth) states:
"The realm of Mahāyāna roots of goodness is equal and free from the names of disparagement or humility."
Women and those with physical impairments,
as well as those of the two vehicles' lineage, do not arise there.
This refers to a land of pure Śrāvakas.
The sentient beings in this place exclusively study the Hīnayāna;
they are immediately reborn in that land.
This refers to those born through the two middle grades among the nine grades of birth.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"There is a wondrous and pure land."
Transcending the three realms, all arhats shall be born therein.
Regarding the "mixed lands of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna":
the sentient beings in this place study both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna together.
They are reborn in that land immediately;
these are those who are born in the middle grade of the middle class and those born in the three grades of the lower class among the nine grades of birth.
As stated in the *Sūtra on Rebirth in the Middle Grade*:
"Filially supporting one's parents and practicing worldly benevolence and compassion."
He encountered a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra),
who expounded for him the forty-eight great vows and so forth; among these vows:
He heard various teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna;
although he attained the fruit of Arhatship upon reaching that place,
he later turned his mind toward the Mahāyāna.
The three classes of the lower grade likewise hear the forty-eight great vows,
or they hear the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
Or, by recollecting Amitābha Buddha,
they are born in that land,
where all give rise to the bodhicitta.
In this general discourse, there are these three lands.
If one were to analyze them in detail,
it concerns the conduct that sentient beings initiate.
Since there are already a thousand distinctions,
there will likewise be ten thousand variations in the lands seen upon rebirth.
If one interprets it in this way,
then in various sūtras and śāstras,
it is sometimes judged to be retribution (vipāka).
Some may judge this to be a transformation body;
there is no difficulty or contradiction in either case.
One simply needs to know that these are the practices of all Buddhas.
It possesses both the retribution and transformation lands.
As stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the transformation land is produced through preparatory application (*prayoga*).
They manifest in their true bodies as retribution or transformation; in all cases,
they seek to bring sentient beings to fulfillment.
Thus, the lands are not established in vain,
and practices are not cultivated in vain;
one need only have faith in the Buddha’s words.
By relying on the sutras and maintaining focused mindfulness,
one will immediately attain rebirth there;
furthermore, there is no need to deliberate upon whether this is a retribution body or a transformation body.
Question: It can be understood that the principle of the Dharmakāya and the Pure Land is all-pervasive.
The two lands of retribution and transformation must have distinct boundaries;
since the Western [Pure Land] possesses both the land of retribution and the land of transformation.
On what textual evidence is this based?
The answer is:
the two lands of retribution and transformation.
Some have boundaries, while others have no boundaries;
this is like the true retribution land within the lands of retribution.
Thus there are no boundaries;
it is said that the Tathāgata’s practice was perfected over eighty thousand [kalpas],
and his time was fulfilled over three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
The two teachings are uniquely complete,
the five divisions are clearly manifest,
and their characteristics exhaustively reach the drops of the ocean.
Having thoroughly exhausted the dust of the mountains,
the three insights are already radiant,
and the two types of wisdom shine forth together.
It is like the dragon’s roar being answered by the clouds and the tiger’s cry followed by the wind;
how could it be that because their precious ornaments differ,
they cannot be encompassed within the same boundaries?
In this land, only the Buddha himself beholds its excellence;
even Bodhisattvas have not yet set eyes upon it.
As for the Land of Retribution:
That is to say, below it were pillars of vajra,
above it was ground of polished lapis lazuli,
and its outer perimeter was surrounded by railings of the seven treasures.
Within, it was filled with a clear pool of the eight virtues;
jeweled rafts floated amidst the emerald groves,
and precious nets draped over the ornate halls.
Since his person is replete with myriad virtues,
his land is likewise overflowing with manifold excellences; such is this land.
Thus, there are indeed boundaries.
Within this transformed land,
it is established by the power of the Great Compassionate Vow.
Equal to the realm of sentient beings,
there is nowhere it does not pervade;
thus, it has no boundaries.
If one considers the body as a means of transforming sentient beings,
it is born anew in every life and enters nirvana again and again.
Thus there are boundaries and frontiers.
As for the Western Land being the land of retribution,
this is set forth in the *Mahāyāna-saṃbhoga-sūtra* (The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Common Nature).
The Sūtra states:
The Bodhisattva Jñānaprabha asked the Buddha, the World-Honored One:
"What is the reward body (saṃbhogakāya) of the Tathāgata?"
The Buddha said:
"That which you now see as me is the reward body (saṃbhogakāya) of the Tathāgata."
Furthermore, there are those who have attained perfect awakening, as well as those who shall attain perfect awakening, within pure buddha-fields.
"All of them are [in] the reward body (saṃbhogakāya).
The commentary states:
"They attain Buddhahood within the pure land."
That which is judged to be the *pāka* (maturation) is the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body),
not the actual *vipākakāya* (retribution body).
If one manifests a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya),
it is precisely a subtle transformation body.
As the Sūtra says:
That you now see me is the reward body (saṃbhogakāya); thus,
even within this defiled land, one perceives the reward body.
This very sutra states:
"One attains Buddhahood amidst the five turbidities.
There are the periods of the True Dharma, the Semblance Dharma, and the Final Dharma."
This refers to the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) and transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya).
The sūtras judge that all those who attain buddhahood within impure lands do so as transformation-bodies;
yet, it further states, "You see me now."
This is the reward body (saṃbhogakāya). Since one can see the reward body within a defiled land,
for what reason can one not see the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) within a pure land?
Thus, we know that both the pure and impure lands possess both bodies [the Dharma-body and the transformation-body].
As for the statement that this is a land of transformation (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*),
it appears in the *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*.
The Sūtra says:
"Good son, the lifespan of Amitābha Buddha is immeasurable."
Even hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas must have an end;
yet after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
the True Dharma shall remain in the world.
Equal to the lifespan of the Buddha. Good son,
after the extinction of Amitābha Buddha’s True Dharma...
After the middle watch of the night,
when the light of dawn appeared,
the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara...
Beneath the Bodhi tree, he attained equal and perfect enlightenment,
receiving the title Tathāgata Universal Radiance Merit Mountain King.
In that buddha-land, there are no names for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
That buddha-land is named Adorned by the Universal Gathering of All Jewels.
After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Samantaprabhāsa-guṇa and the extinction of his True Dharma, [this land will arise].
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta shall immediately attain Buddhahood in that land,
receiving the title Tathāgata Supratiṣṭhita-ratnarāja.
The land, radiance, lifespan,
and even the duration of the Dharma shall be identical and without difference.
Furthermore, the *Dhāraṇī-sūtra of the King of Drum-Sounds* states that Amitābha Buddha had parents, children,
and [disciples such as] Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and Devadatta.
Second, regarding the inclusion or exclusion [of these lands] within the three realms (*tridhātu*):
A question is asked:
"The Land of Reward (*vipākakṣetra*) is pure and sublime, utterly transcending the three realms of existence (*tribhava*)."
As for the sentient beings to be transformed, they have already transcended the stage of分段 (pariccheda-bheda) birth;
since this land emerges from the triple world,
this principle is also easy to believe.
Although the transformed land is pure,
its purity is not yet sublime;
furthermore, the sentient beings being transformed still remain at the stage prior to the grounds.
Is this land included within the three realms,
or is it not so included?
The answer is:
If discussed in terms of the Buddha,
he is wondrously transcendent beyond the three realms;
if viewed from the perspective of sentient beings...
It possesses two meanings:
inclusion and non-inclusion.
First, to clarify inclusion:
If one considers those ordinary beings and those in training who have attained the first three fruits and are reborn there,
they are subsumed within the triple world (*tridhātu*),
because such sentient beings have not yet transcended the triple world.
Question: How can this meaning be known? Answer:
As stated in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*:
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One..."
Since that land lacks Mount Sumeru and the like,
upon what do the Four Heavenly Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven rely for their abode?
The Buddha replied:
"They abide by the power of karma.
Once there were humans, and subsequently the Four Heavenly Kings and others appeared."
It should be known that this is precisely the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, this same sutra says:
He addressed Maitreya:
"Do you see, from the earth upward,
even unto the Śuddhāvāsa Heavens?"
"Have you seen all the matters of adornment?
He replied, "I have seen them."
It should be understood that this refers specifically to the realms of desire and form,
but does not include the formless realm.
Question: For what reason is the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) not discussed? Answer:
The intention was to praise the wondrous colors and adornments of the Pure Land in order to lead sentient beings to be reborn there;
that is why it is not discussed here.
Yet its substance exists.
A question is asked:
"This body and that land—"
Question: Since they are both within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), for what reason does the Great Sage encourage people to be reborn there? Answer:
Although the name "desire realm" (kāmadhātu) is the same,
its meaning is distinct.
This refers to the desire realm in this context.
It possesses two meanings:
first, there is manifest desire;
second, there is latent desire.
Due to the presence of these two factors,
there arises the defilement of male and female,
as craving pursues forms and sounds.
They take pleasure in dwelling within the burning house of the three realms of existence.
As for those in the desire realm of the Western [continent],
they possess only the seeds of desire.
There is no superior desire of the mind.
Since there is no superior desire of the mind,
there are no faults such as those mentioned above.
Furthermore, there is neither an unwholesome mind nor an indeterminate mind;
there is only a wholesome mind.
Thus, it is said in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* regarding the eighteen kinds of perfect purity:
In the Pure Land, there is only pleasant sensation;
there is no painful or neutral sensation.
As the Mahābherī-hāraka-parivarta Sūtra states:
Painful feeling is unwholesome;
pleasant feeling is wholesome;
neutral feeling is indeterminate.
Since there is only a virtuous mind,
there is no ground for the arising of evil.
Therefore, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* says:
In the land of Amitābha,
there is not even a space the size of a hair’s breadth where evil can be committed,
even though it is said to be within the realm of desire.
How could they be the same? As it is with the desire realm,
so it is with the form realm as well.
Question: The Pure Land is exceptionally sublime;
all beings look up to it with joy and admiration.
If you wish to encourage others to be reborn there,
why must it be judged as being subsumed within the three realms?
The answer is:
This is the determination of the Sūtra;
it does not concern persons.
Furthermore, if it were subsumed within the three realms, [it would follow that...].
Sentient beings who have not yet severed the afflictions of the three realms can be reborn there immediately;
as for those who have transcended the three realms— namely,
ordinary worldlings and those in training— [they cannot].
This is a case of being beyond [the realm of] differentiation.
It is not possible to take those sentient beings within the three realms,
all of whom are fully possessed of afflictions.
It causes one to be born within the Reward Land outside the triple world.
Because one remains within the triple world,
rebirth there is easy.
Because they still possess the unsurpassed aspiration,
they ultimately do not regress. Question:
Since it is subsumed within the three realms,
it ought to regress;
how then can it be called "non-regressive"?
The answer is:
The designation "three realms" is general;
it does not refer to only one kind.
Just as in the eastern world-system of Abhirati,
there is a Jambudvīpa and a Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
with both men and women.
Yet it is called a Pure Land;
how could it exist outside the triple world?
Since there are women within the triple world, [it must likewise be so here].
Therefore, it is also a realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Could it be the same as the Saṃbhava-kāma-dhātu (the Desire Realm of Endurance)?
That is called a Pure Land (*śuddhakṣetra*), while this is called a Defiled Field (*kliṣṭakṣetra*).
Now, it is judged that these are merely transformed pure lands;
those who transform sentient beings within their realms all reside within the three realms.
If it is a reward pure land that transforms sentient beings outside the [three] realms,
then it transcends the three realms.
This is simply because there are three grades of superiority and inferiority among pure lands.
For example, the world of Abhirati in the east is an inferior pure land.
Because it is mixed with both men and women,
the Western World of Ultimate Bliss is a pure land.
Because it is mixed with those of the two vehicles,
the World of Fragrant Upper (Gandhavatī) in the zenith is a superior pure land.
Because there are no followers of the two vehicles [in those lands],
these three grades of pure lands are all situated within the realm of desire (kāmadhātu).
Because it is a distinct dwelling place for humans and devas:
as for the presence of humans and devas in the world of Abhirati,
it is as stated in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra:
From Jambudvīpa up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Regarding those among humans and devas in the World of Ultimate Bliss,
as stated in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*:
The Buddha said to Maitreya:
"Do you see all the various adornments from the earth up to the five Pure Abodes in the World of Universal Fragrance?"
Regarding "humans and devas," as stated in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra:
"It causes all humans and devas to enter into the practice of the precepts."
Since these possess distinct abodes for humans and devas,
one should know that they are located within the desire realm (kāmadhātu). If they were in the form realm (rūpadhātu), [they would not have such distinctions].
Although there are heavens,
one should know that their abodes are situated within the realm of desire (kāmadhātu).
If one is in the realm of form (rūpadhātu),
although there are devas,
there are no humans.
Because the Form Realm (rūpadhātu) is situated above,
humans are unable to ascend there; furthermore,
if one were to exit beyond the Three Realms (tridhātu), [it would be impossible].
Thus, there would be no distinct abodes for humans and devas.
Just as the Pure Lands have three grades,
so too do the defiled lands have three grades.
As it is said in the sutra:
"To the east of this place, there is a world named Saha."
The soil consists only of sand and gravel in triangular patches;
there are two rains per year,
and the moisture does not penetrate more than five inches.
The sentient beings in that land subsist solely on the seeds of grasses and wear tree bark as clothing;
though they seek them, they cannot obtain them.
Seeking death, they could not find it.
This is a defiled land in the center.
Furthermore, there is another world.
Tigers, wolves, and venomous beasts,
even down to snakes and scorpions,
are all able to fly.
They encounter one another and immediately devour each other,
making no distinction between the virtuous and the wicked; this is a low and defiled land.
In the Sahā world,
Buddhas constantly appear in the world;
there are sentient beings who give rise to the bodhicitta.
The earth produces non-glutinous grain,
and the people possess propriety and righteousness;
this is an upper-grade impure land.
Although the Pure Land has three grades,
all who attain birth therein are never again subject to regression;
likewise, the Impure Land also has three grades.
However, all those who give rise [to such thoughts] will universally regress.
Furthermore, in the Western Pure Land,
there are four causes and conditions.
One progresses alone and does not regress.
First, one does not regress because of long life,
as the Sūtra says:
Because his lifespan lasts for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas,
he shall attain Buddhahood by practicing the path for exactly three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
How much more so for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas!
One regresses from the defiled land because of short life spans.
Second, there are various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
One does not regress because of [the presence of] spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
As the Sūtra says:
"Because one is able to assemble in one place together with such superior and virtuous persons."
The defiled land suffers decline because of the abundance of evil associates.
Third, there are no women,
nor any objects of the six sense faculties.
These are all conditions for advancing on the Path;
therefore, one does not regress.
As the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* says:
Upon seeing forms with the eye, one immediately gives rise to the bodhicitta;
likewise, even when the mind conditions dharmas, one gives rise to the bodhicitta.
This impure land exists because of women.
The objects of the six sense faculties are all conditions for retreating from the Path; therefore, one retreats because of them.
Fourth, because there is only wholesome mind, one does not retreat.
As the sutra says:
"There is not even a patch of ground the size of a hair or a fingernail where evil can be committed;
yet this defiled land regresses because of the presence of evil minds and indeterminate minds."
Second, regarding those who are not included:
if they are bodhisattvas of the first stage and above,
as well as arhats, pratyekabuddhas, or those born into the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
This is not included,
because the underlying tendencies have already been severed and one has emerged from the three realms.
As stated in the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra:
"There is a wondrous and pure land that transcends the triple world."
All Arhats shall be born therein; since the treatise already refers to them as "Arhats."
Regardless of whether one is a learner (śaikṣa),
it is therefore known that a learner who is still living exists within the three realms.
2. Determining Those Who Attain Rebirth. Second, determining those who attain rebirth: at what stage does one obtain rebirth? Question:
It has already been understood that the substance of the land encompasses both the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body).
It is not yet known at what stage of practice a person attains rebirth there.
The answer is:
now, relying upon the sūtras and śāstras.
Thus, according to the Buddha’s intention,
those who practice solely in reliance upon the sūtras and śāstras—
regardless of whether they are ordinary persons or sages, male or female— [attain this].
Even those who have committed the ten evil deeds or the five heinous crimes will have right mindfulness manifest before them at the time of their death.
Those whose minds are not distracted shall all attain rebirth,
with the sole exception of those who slander the Mahāyāna, who shall not attain rebirth.
This is according to the *Contemplation Sūtra*.
If one follows the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*,
those who have committed the five heinous crimes are also excluded.
Question: These two sūtras were both spoken by the same Buddha.
Why does the Mahāyāna sūtra exclude two [aspects],
while the Contemplation Sūtra excludes one?
The answer is:
To first establish prohibitions and later grant exceptions is the constant law of all Buddhas;
this was stated first in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
This is because it extensively explains the causal conditions of the Bhikṣu Dharmākara and clarifies the matters concerning rebirth;
this is stated at the conclusion of the *Contemplation Sūtra*.
This is because it discusses exclusively the matter of rebirth.
A question is asked:
As the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
"All sentient beings who are born [there] shall abide entirely within the group of those destined for right certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Furthermore, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:"
Śāriputra, those beings born in the land of Ultimate Bliss are all *avaivartika*.
According to these two sutras,
one must have attained at least the tenth stage of understanding (*daśabhūmi*) before being able to attain rebirth there.
Why is it said that even those who have committed the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes can all attain rebirth?
The answer is:
those in the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and those who are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) are both described as "not falling back."
The term "non-retrogression" is general and is not restricted to the stage of the ten understandings;
now, we shall rely upon the sūtras and śāstras.
There are four kinds of liberation.
The first is non-retrogression through mindfulness,
which refers to those in the eighth stage and above.
Second is non-retrogression in practice,
which refers to those from the first bhūmi upward.
Third is non-retrogression in status.
This refers to those who have already attained the stage of the ten understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*).
The fourth is the place of non-retrogression,
which refers to the Pure Land of the West.
Therefore, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
"In that land, there are no such things as the names 'those of false certainty' or 'those of no certainty.
Furthermore, among the forty-eight great vows, it says:"
If, when I attain Buddhahood,
the humans and devas in my land do not abide in the stage of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma), may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
"If I do not attain perfect awakening until all beings have surely reached nirvāṇa"—
this statement regarding non-retrogression encompasses four types [of bodhisattvas].
It would be better to cite one instance of non-retrogression to definitively exclude the three [other cases].
Question: Regarding the discussion of non-retrogression...
One must rely upon the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*).
How does one attain non-retrogression by depending on these bases?
The answer is:
There is no regression from the stages of practice because there are no afflictions within;
there is no regression from one's station because there are no external objects.
Each relies on a single meaning;
what is there to be surprised about? He asked:
That the first three stages are non-retrogressive is clearly evidenced by the sūtras and śāstras;
this may thus be trusted.
Since there is no textual evidence for the non-retrogression of the stage,
how can one gain conviction?
The answer is as follows:
Now, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* is cited as evidence.
As that treatise sets forth six types of persons by nature (*gotra*),
the first is the one subject to falling away (*parihāṇa*).
The second is reflection;
the third is protection;
the fourth is the stage.
Fifth is advancement;
sixth is immovability. These refer, for example, to those of the nature of regression.
Even if one attains arhatship,
one may still fall back;
this extends even to the arising of afflictions associated with the path of cultivation within the three realms.
Because their faculties are weak by nature,
although this person’s constitution is of a regressive faculty,
if this person is among humans in the desire realm, [they may fall away].
Upon encountering the five conditions for retrogression, one immediately regresses.
However, if one is born among the gods of the six desire heavens, or within the form or formless realms,
these five conditions for retrogression do not exist.
They do not regress;
because there are no conditions for regression within that state, they never regress.
The five factors leading to decline are:
first, chronic illness;
second, long-distance travel.
Third, reciting the sūtras;
fourth, attending to the physical needs of the community;
fifth, reconciling disputes.
These five types exist only among human beings;
they do not exist among gods or other [beings].
Although the three practices such as reciting sutras are virtuous deeds, they should be set aside for the sake of entering into contemplation.
Therefore, they retreat.
By analogy with this case,
other instances may be understood in the same way.
Just as all ordinary beings,
although they may recollect the Buddha,
have not yet reached the stage of the ten understandings.
Because they are ordinary beings outside [the stages of realization], their nature is that of those subject to regression.
If such a person is within this defiled land of Sahā, [they are subject to falling back].
Because one encounters the five conditions for retrogression, one immediately regresses;
if one is born in the Western Land,
because the five conditions for retrogression do not exist, one does not regress.
The five conditions for decline are:
first, a short life and much illness;
second, the presence of women and the arising of defilement regarding the six sense objects.
Third is the person of evil conduct, namely, an evil associate (*pāpamitra*).
Fourth is an unwholesome or indeterminate state of mind.
Fifth is the constant failure to encounter a Buddha.
In the Pure Land, these five conditions for regression do not exist;
therefore, there is ultimately no falling back.
This is cited from the sacred teachings.
It is clear that the state of non-retrogression is realized at that place.
Furthermore, according to two sutras,
it is stated that those who attain rebirth there achieve non-retrogression.
It does not say that those who do not fall back attain rebirth.
Therefore, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
"Those who are born in that land..."
All dwell within the category of those destined for right determination (samyaktva-niyāma).
Why is this? Because in that land, even the names of those in the category of wrong determination (mithyātva-niyāma) or the indeterminate category (aniyata-niyāma) do not exist.
A minor sūtra also says:
"All sentient beings who are born are all *avaivartika*."
It does not say that those who are non-retrogressive (avaivartika) attain rebirth there.
It is like those in this world who possess the three types of sensation;
if they were born in that land, they would have neither suffering nor equanimity.
There is only pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā),
because in that place there are no two types of feeling. Question:
As the *Contemplation Sūtra* states:
"Those of the highest grade in the highest birth,
upon being born, reach that land."
One immediately awakens to the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). This is precisely the eighth stage (bhūmi);
one should know this.
Those of inferior grade are born [in the Pure Land] after having already attained the stage of the ten understandings (daśa-adhimukti);
if they are before the ten understandings, they are not so.
Not only does this contradict the sacred teachings,
but the disparity in status is also far too great.
He replied:
Not so. There are likewise four kinds of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
First, by taking the teaching as an object,
one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas;
this refers to all ordinary beings.
Furthermore, those at the stage of the ten levels of faith read Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras,
giving rise to the understanding of non-arising.

This is precisely the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). Second, through the contemplation of conditions, one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*),
which refers to the stages from the ten levels of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti*) up to the ten levels of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).
This refers to practicing the contemplation of the three natures of non-essence and realizing that all phenomena are unarisen;
this is precisely the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
Third, by realizing the principle, one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*),
which refers to the stages from the first bhūmi upward;
this occurs through the realization of the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the two-fold emptiness that pervades the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
This is precisely the cultivation of wisdom.
Fourth, regarding the attainment of the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) according to stages:
this refers to the eighth stage and above.
By attaining the simultaneous practice of the ultimate and the conventional,
one possesses non-conceptual wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*);
this is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*).
Since the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) applies to all four of these,
how could one possibly adhere to only one?
Regarding the high-ranking judgment of the others:
it is as Master Yuan judged the "Highest Birth of the Highest Grade" as spanning from the fourth bhūmi to the eighth bhūmi.
If, according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
Bodhisattvas of the fourth stage undergo the birth-and-death of causal conditions within the transformational body (*pariṇāmika-kāya*).
The West is the realm of *paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa* (segmented birth and death).
How could one cause a Bodhisattva who has attained *pariṇāmi-jāti-maraṇa* (transformative birth and death) to instead undergo segmented birth and death?
Therefore, the *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* states:
One should know that although the lifespan of Amitābha Buddha is immeasurable,
he will eventually enter parinirvāṇa.
Although the lifespan of sentient beings may be immeasurable,
they must inevitably die;
as the Shorter Amitābha Sūtra states:
Sentient beings are also called Amitābha.
Now, based on the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*,
the persons born in the nine grades are distinguished.
As for the great virtuous ones of antiquity, such as Master Yuan and others,
their assessment of individuals based on their realization of the fruit places their status too high.
Judging persons now by their causes,
their status is somewhat lower than that of those who attain the "Highest Birth of the Superior Class" mentioned above.
By giving rise to three kinds of mind,
one immediately attains rebirth there.
As for those three kinds of mind:
The first is the mind of utmost sincerity;
the second is the profound mind;
the third is the mind of dedication and aspiration.
These three minds, according to the *Awakening of Faith*,
are determined to be at the initial stage of the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti*).
As stated in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*:
"The arousal of the mind through the perfection of faith" occurs at the conclusion of the stage of the ten faiths.
One gives rise to three kinds of mind upon first entering the stage of the ten understandings (*daśa-vyavasthāna*).
These three minds are:
The first is the straightforward mind (*ṛjukacitta*).
This refers to maintaining right mindfulness of the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness).
It is precisely what is called the "mind of utmost sincerity" in the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*.
Sincerity and the straightforward mind are identical in meaning, differing only in name,
as clarified in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra.
The two practices at the beginning of the Pure Land practice hall both involve three minds,
which are identical to those in the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
Upon examining the various sūtras and śāstras,
one finds that they all clarify that the beginning of every practice must necessarily give rise to these three minds; thus,
it should be known.
These three minds are the beginning of the myriad practices.
Since they are the initial stage of the myriad practices,
how could one who gives rise to them fail to realize non-arising immediately and reach the eighth stage?
The second is the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*);
the *Amitābha Sūtra* also refers to it as the profound mind.
The third is the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇācitta*).
The *Amitābha Sūtra* is titled "The Mind of Dedication and Aspiration.
Without great compassion,
one is unable to generate the aspiration for dedication.
This is also a case where the meaning is the same while the names differ.
Since the three minds in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* arise at the conclusion of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), [they correspond to this].

It should be understood that the "highest birth of the highest grade" described in the *Contemplation Sūtra* is clearly realized at the initial stage of the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti*).
As for the statement that one attains the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) upon reaching that [stage],
this refers to the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas through the contemplation of conditions (pratyaya).
If, as Master Yuan has judged, Bodhisattvas of the fourth stage are those who attain the highest grade of the highest birth,
how could they possibly reach that realm and, without passing through any period of time, immediately realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas?
From the fourth stage to the eighth stage,
because half an asaṃkhyeya kalpa has elapsed.
As for those of superior faculties who are born from middle [capacity]:
Regarding the initial stage of the ten faiths,
the Sūtra states:
"Profoundly believe in cause and effect."
Because they do not slander the Mahāyāna.
If they have not yet reached the stage of the ten faiths,
they remain within the group of those fixed in error.
This constitutes a lack of faith in cause and effect,
as well as the slandering of the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, within the stage of faith, there are ten mental states.
The former refers to the mind of faith.
As for the statement that one attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) after being born in that land for one minor kalpa (*antarakalpa*),
this pertains to the contemplation of principle (*tattva*).
One attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Because those days and months are long,
the Sūtra says:
In the Land of Ultimate Bliss,
one day and night is equivalent to one kalpa in the Sahā world.
If, as Master Daoyuan judges, one who has attained the first bhūmi is such [a person],
how is it that after only a single minor kalpa,
they immediately reach the eighth bhūmi?
From the first stage to the eighth stage constitutes one great asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
As for those who attain rebirth in the lower grade of the superior class:
This always refers to ordinary persons who, prior to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), have performed all manner of wholesome deeds;
it includes everyone from those who merely take refuge in the Triple Gem to those who have already received the Bodhisattva precepts.
The Sūtra says:
"They also believe in cause and effect and do not slander the Mahāyāna."
It simply means to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment;
that is, to give rise to the initial bodhicitta of the stage of the ten faiths and thereby enter the stage of non-fixedness.
Having been born in that land,
after three minor kalpas have passed,
one attains the first bhūmi.
This refers to counting the kalpas of that world,
not counting the kalpas of this world;
for example, one kalpa of the Sahā world.
A single day and night in the realm of Sukhāvatī corresponds to three minor kalpas;
by principle, this is the first bhūmi.
If, as Master Yuan has judged, the ten stages of understanding (daśa-vyākaraṇa) are indeed these,
how is it that after three minor kalpas one reaches the first stage (prathamā-bhūmi)?
From the stage of the ten understandings (*daśa-vijñapti*) up to the first ground (*prathama-bhūmi*) constitutes the first asaṃkhyeya-kalpa.
This comprises the first three categories.
These are all Mahāyāna practitioners;
among them, those of the three grades of the middle class are mostly Śrāvaka practitioners.
Regarding those born in the middle grade through superior means:
this refers to the latter four of the seven stages of expedient means within the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
This refers to the stages of *uṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, *kṣānti*, and *laukikāgradharma*.
As the Sūtra says:
"One who upholds the five precepts..."
Up to the point that they are free from all faults and evils.
This person, by virtue of attaining the four factors conducive to penetration and the dhyāna of the future life (anāgāmyadhyāna).
Because one has subdued the afflictions of the desire realm,
the afflictions of breaking the precepts and evil karma do not arise;
for it is the afflictions of breaking the precepts and evil karma that reside within the desire realm.
Those who are born in that land and immediately attain arhatship obtain the four fruits of the śramaṇa in a single lifetime;
these are the individuals who realize parinirvāṇa in the present life (dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin).
According to the judgment of Master Daoyuan,
these are the practitioners in training who have attained the three fruits, such as *srotāpanna*,
and have thus achieved the fruits of the Hīnayāna.
Although there is no fixed period of time,
it is ultimately judged to be too high.
As for those born in the middle grade of the intermediate state:
This occurs after the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-vastu-sthāpana*) and within the first three preliminary applications (*pūrvāṅga-prayoga*).
As the Sūtra says:
One observes the eightfold precepts for one day and one night,
up to observing the full set of precepts for one day and one night,
with one's dignified deportment remaining flawless.
Because this person is in a state of distracted mind and has not yet attained meditative concentration,
there is no antidote for their transgressions of the precepts and their afflictions.
One cannot maintain the precepts for a long duration;
the observance of proper conduct must be flawless for at least one day and one night.
Even if one subsequently violates a minor precept, [the prior observance remains valid].
They shall also attain rebirth there;
having been born in that land, after half a kalpa has passed,
they will attain arhatship.
This person is also one who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life,
due to the length of their lifespan;
as explained by Master Yuǎn.
Among these four stages, such as the stage of "heat" (ūṣmagata) and so forth,
these are the persons belonging to these four stages.
Having attained future dhyāna and suppressed the afflictions of the desire realm,
how does one maintain the precepts?
To obtain [this] for only one day and one night without transgression is still too much.
As for those of the middle grade who are born below:
Prior to the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-viṣaya-sthāpana*) in the Hīnayāna,
all ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who have attained wholesome states across the various destinies and have received the five precepts.
The Sūtra says:
"Filially support one's parents and practice benevolence and compassion in the world."
Since one has not yet attained the contemplative practice for entering the Way,
one should properly cultivate worldly benevolence and compassion.
The rest is as previously determined.
As Master Daoyuan has judged,
these constitute the five contemplations for settling the mind,
up to the stage of the general characteristics of the foundations of mindfulness.
These three types of persons may attain either the wisdom derived from hearing or the wisdom derived from reflection.
Or one may attain the wisdom of cultivation.
Why then would one merely practice worldly benevolence and compassion,
or filially support one's parents?
This [classification] is still too high.
If we discuss the three grades of the lower class,
they comprise all ordinary people who give rise to evil.
They commit only the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes,
even misappropriating the property of the permanently resident Sangha,
all without any sense of shame or remorse.
Even if one were to study and receive the precepts from another,
they would break them as soon as they received them.
If such individuals encounter a virtuous friend at the time of death, [they may attain liberation].
By intensely generating the bodhicitta and maintaining the continuity of right mindfulness before one,
one will immediately attain rebirth there.
If one does not encounter a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra),
one will be unable to fully resolve the mind toward enlightenment (bodhicitta) and will certainly fall into hell.
Therefore, the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* states:
"This person should fall into hell, where they will undergo suffering without end for many kalpas.
However, when the retribution of sentient beings is exhausted—
With evil karma as one's enemy,
manifold sufferings converge in competition;
even ten recitations are extremely difficult to accomplish.
If one achieves this,
one will certainly attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
Furthermore, regarding the two paths of good and evil:
It is as steep as a turning palm:
if one looks upward, one immediately attains rebirth in the Pure Land;
if one looks downward, one immediately enters hell.
At this time, one must rely solely on the power of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
If a person violates the precepts, [they cannot succeed].
A sense of shame and remorse arose in his mind;
he repented according to the Mahāyāna sūtras and attained signs that his transgressions were extinguished.
Those who single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and those who practice meditative contemplation will both be reborn among the first two classes of aspirants.
This does not enter into the discussion of the lowest class of practitioners.
As Master Yuan has judged,
this refers to ordinary, mundane worldlings.
Question: At the gateway to the Pure Land,
ordinary beings and sages alike proceed together.
I do not yet know whose intention this doctrine represents. Who, precisely, is its author?
He replied:
Contemplating the intent behind Vaidhī’s request and the Tathāgata’s response,
it is stated that this is solely for the sake of all ordinary beings in future ages who are harmed by the thieves of affliction.
He expounded upon the practice of purifying karma and exhorted people to be reborn [in the Pure Land],
regardless of whether they were bodhisattvas.
